You can use should in if-clauses instead of a Present or Unreal Past to talk about a hypothetical situation in a conditional clause. The condition is possible but unlikely.
Should you see a blockbuster movie this weekend, expect it to have special effects.
You use should in an if-clause to suggest that a condition is possible but unlikely.

Structure:
If + should + verb … , would/will + verb

Example:
If you should agree that FX movies are for you, then you would know that they abound these days.
This structure has the same meaning as If by any chance.
You can also omit if in certain contexts and start the sentence with should. It is usually quite formal.
Should you want more after the first thrilling adventure, a sequel would prove to be just the thing to entice you the second time around.
Should a director want even more control, his computer would allow him to edit  scenes until they are perfect.

When you talk about two actions linked together, you normally use two verbs. The first verb follows the rules of conjugation for the sentence, while the second verb can be a verb in the -ing form or a bare infinitive.
I've noticed more and more people doze off in the artier films these days.
Verbs connected with observation like see, notice, feel, hear, watch can be followed by either an -ing form or a bare infinitive.

Example:
I've noticed more people dozing/doze off at the cinema these days.
You normally use the -ing form when you suggest that an action is in progress, while the bare infinitive suggests that the action is completed.

images.text: Should you see a blockbuster movie this weekend, expect it to have special effects. If by any chance it is a sequel, you'd better expect twice as many. If you should agree that FX movies are for you, then you would know that they abound these days. Trifling little affairs of the heart on film, without movie magic seem dull to many. I've noticed more and more people doze off in the artier films these days.

Today, when people go to the movies, they want to be impressed. One way to impress moviegoers is by letting them have their fill of special effects. Special effects make the unbelievable seem believable. Dinosaurs live again, spaceships battle to save the planet, and whole cities disappear in the blink of an eye – all thanks to special effects. Should you want more after the first thrilling adventure, a sequel would prove to be just the thing to entice you the second time around.

Special effects have been part of moviemaking almost from the start. If by any chance you look up how they were done you'd find they were originally called  "tricks"  because some ideas had actually been stolen from stage magicians. Watching FX scenes play, you often notice stop motion and forced perspective effects. These are among the oldest. In today's special effects, you see artists use new methods developed with modern technology. For example, green screens let moviemakers shoot completely separate scenes and then combine them into one. Should a director want even more control, his computer would allow him to edit  scenes until they are perfect. So whether we're watching spaceships explode, giant bugs invade from outer space, or cool morphing robots, special effects will always make going to the movies a more exciting and magical experience.
